=== 2026-9-9 ASL's Reply to Exceptions.pdf ===
                                    SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                       PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                                    §
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC                                 §
AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICE                                 §         BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR                                    §
CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND                               §
NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY                                 §                            OF
EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                            §
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN                           §
BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,                                §        ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,                                       §
MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS,                              §
SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                              §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                                       §

     AMERICAN STEWARDS OF LIBERTY’S REPLY TO COMMISSION STAFF AND
         APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

         COMES NOW, American Stewards of Liberty (ASL) and files its Reply to the Exceptions

 to the Proposal for Decision (PDF) of: (1) Commission Staff (Staff); and (2) Oncor Electric

 Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation’s (collectively, the

 Applicants), and in support thereof, shows as follows.

                                             I.    INTRODUCTION

         ASL agrees with the PFD’s analysis, findings and conclusions that Applicants failed to

 carry their burden to establish that the Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake

 projects comprising Import Path 2 are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or

 safety of the public under PURA § 37.056(a). 1 ASL further agrees with the PFD’s findings and

 conclusion that Applicants failed as a matter of law to comply with the notice requirements in

 Docket No. 59475.




 1
  Because the issue of need was jointly considered for Import Path 2, the PFD’s determination on need applies to both
 Docket No. 59182 and Docket No. 59475.
         On the statutory factor of need, the PFD correctly recognizes the distinction between a

regional transmission planning recommendation and the project-specific showing of need required

to amend a certificate of convenience and necessity. Unlike the CREZ legislation, HB 5066 did

not legislatively determine that any particular transmission facility was necessary, nor did it exempt

the resulting projects from the needs requirements of PURA § 37.056. Applicants therefore

remained obligated to prove that Import Path 2 itself is necessary. The SOAH ALJs correctly

concluded they did not.

        The Exceptions of both Staff and Applicants largely ask the Commission to substitute

ERCOT’s prior planning determinations for that statutory showing.             Staff argues that the

Commission’s approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) and subsequent approval of

Import Path 1 effectively resolve the need question here. Applicants similarly argue that ERCOT’s

continued inclusion of the 765-kV import paths in subsequent planning models forecloses the

PFD’s consideration of changed circumstances. Neither Staff nor Applicants’ arguments respond

to the evidentiary deficiencies identified by the SOAH ALJs. The question is not whether ERCOT

once recommended three 765-kV import paths, or whether those paths continue to appear in

ERCOT planning models. The question is whether the evidence in record establishes that this

particular billion dollar infrastructure commitment is necessary under PURA § 37.056. The PFD

correctly concluded it does not.

        The PFD’s conclusion rests on several independent grounds:

        •        Applicants did not establish independent need for Import Path 2;

        •        the load assumptions underlying the PBRP have been materially undermined by
                 subsequent developments;

        •        the Far West generic transmission constraints (GTCs) do not validate those
                 underlying load assumptions;



ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                       Page 2
            •        the record does not establish that sufficient power will be available to flow west
                    from Bell County East; and

           •        substantial new generation being developed within the Permian Basin provides
                    credible evidence of an alternative that could reduce or eliminate the need for this
                    unprecedented transmission expansion.

None of the Exceptions cures those deficiencies.

           The PFD’s notice determination provides a separate and independent basis for denying the

application in Docket No. 59475. Applicants’ Exceptions attempt to minimalize these fundamental

due process deficiencies by pointing to prior Commission practice and suggesting that any defect

can simply be cured through some undefined “additional process.” The PFD correctly recognized

that “additional process” is not available once the transmission line routes have been selected, the

application filed, discovery completed, testimony submitted, and the hearing concluded.

Accordingly, the Commission should adopt the PFD’s determinations on both need and notice.

         II.    REPLY TO COMMISSION STAFF’S EXCEPTIONS REGARDING NEED

A.         Prior approval of the PBRP and Import Path 1 does not establish that Import Path 2
           independently satisfies PURA § 37.056.

           Staff principally argues that because the Commission recently determined in the Import

Path 1 proceedings that the PBRP establishes a need for additional service in the Permian Basin,

it is “only logical” to conclude that Import Path 2 is another necessary component of the solution.2

Staff’s argument conflates regional need for additional service with the statutory necessity of a

particular CCN project.

           The PFD correctly rejected that approach. HB 5066 directed ERCOT to develop a

reliability plan for the Permian Basin. It did not legislatively determine that each facility ultimately

included in that plan was necessary under PURA § 37.056. That distinction is particularly evident


2
    Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 9 (Sept. 2, 2026) (Staff’s Exceptions).


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                                   Page 3
 when HB 5066 is compared to the CREZ legislation. There, the Legislature expressly determined

the necessity of a comprehensive transmission buildout and altered the ordinary statutory need

inquiry. No comparable language appears in HB 5066. Accordingly, as a simple matter of

statutory construction, Applicants were required to demonstrate that Import Path 2 independently

satisfies § 37.056. 3

           Staff’s reliance on the Commission’s recent approval of Import Path 1 does not alter

Applicants’ burden in this proceeding. The Commission’s determination that the Permian Basin

requires additional service does not answer whether this particular import path is necessary,

particularly where ERCOT studied the three import paths principally as an integrated solution and

the record does not contain a study establishing the independent necessity of Import Path 2.

           Indeed, Staff’s reasoning illustrates the very problem identified by the PFD. If a finding

of regional need under the PBRP automatically establishes the necessity of every project included

in the plan, then the project-specific inquiry required by § 37.056 becomes largely meaningless.

HB 5066 contains no language authorizing that result.

B.         “Great weight” does not make ERCOT’s recommendation dispositive.

           Staff next argues that the PFD failed to give ERCOT’s recommendation the “great weight”

required by 16 TAC § 25.101. Staff emphasizes that ERCOT need not provide a witness before

its recommendation receives great weight and criticizes the PFD’s observation that no ERCOT

representative testified. 4 But the ALJs did not conclude that ERCOT’s recommendation is entitled

to no consideration merely because ERCOT did not sponsor a witness. The relevant point is that

“great weight” is not conclusive weight and does not relieve Applicants of their statutory burden




3
    PFD at 87-88.
4
    Staff’s Exceptions at 10-11.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                      Page 4
 of proof. A recommendation remains subject to evaluation against the evidentiary record before

the Commission.

        That distinction is particularly important here because the record contains evidence that

circumstances underlying the PBRP have materially changed since its approval:

        •        ERCOT itself subsequently changed its methodology for evaluating officer-letter
                 and data-center loads;

        •        the Legislature enacted SB 6 to impose additional credibility requirements on large-
                 load interconnections; and

        •        substantial new generation has been announced or is being developed within the
                 Permian Basin.

        The Commission cannot give meaningful effect to its obligation under PURA § 37.056 if

“great weight” requires it to disregard contrary evidence developed in the CCN proceeding. To

simply disregard contrary evidence would constitute legal error.

        Nor does the absence of an ERCOT witness strengthen Staff’s already legally tenuous

position.    To the contrary, Applicants seek extraordinary reliance on ERCOT’s planning

determinations while no ERCOT witness appeared to explain how the subsequent changes

identified in this record affect the assumptions underlying the PBRP. The SOAH ALJs were both

entitled and legally required to consider the recommendation alongside the evidence actually

presented and tested at hearing.

C.      Staff’s reliance on Mr. Poole’s testimony does not cure the PFD’s concerns.

        Staff’s Exceptions go so far as to attempt to undermine the credibility of John Poole, its

own witness, by arguing that his acknowledgment that reevaluation of load demand might be

warranted was given too much weight. Even more glaring, Staff attempts to have it both ways,

simultaneously arguing that Mr. Poole’s ultimate opinion that Import Path 2 is needed for




ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                      Page 5
 reliability, import capability, the Far West GTC exit strategy, and wholesale competition was given

too little weight.5

            But Mr. Poole’s acknowledgment is significant precisely because it confirms the central

concern identified by the PFD: the load assumptions underlying this unprecedented transmission

expansion warrant reevaluation. Mr. Poole’s ultimate support for the project does not erase that

concession, notwithstanding Staff’s disingenuous arguments to the contrary.

            More importantly, the burden belongs to Applicants. The fact that Mr. Poole ultimately

agreed with ERCOT’s recommendation does not supply the missing analysis identified by the

PFD. Mr. Poole’s conclusion does nothing to: (i) establish the durability of the PBRP load forecast;

(ii) demonstrate the independent necessity of Import Path 2; (iii) establish that sufficient power

will be available to flow west from Bell County East; or (iv) determine whether new Permian

generation could reduce or eliminate the need for the project.

D.          ERCOT’s continued inclusion of the 765-kV paths in later planning models does not
            answer the PFD’s concerns.

            Staff argues that “changed circumstances” cannot undermine need because ERCOT has not

withdrawn its recommendation and the 2025 RTP continued to include the 765-kV STEP. 6 But

continued inclusion is not the same thing as a new determination of project-specific need based on

the changed circumstances identified by the PFD.

            Staff’s argument strains credulity. The PFD did not merely identify a later planning

document that reached a different conclusion. It identified changes bearing directly upon the

assumptions used to justify the original project. ERCOT revised its treatment of large-load

forecasts precisely because experience showed that projected loads were not materializing at the



5
    Id. at 11.
6
    Id. at 12.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                     Page 6
 rates previously assumed. Yet there is no evidence that ERCOT reran the PBRP analysis using

those revised assumptions to determine whether Import Path 2 remained independently necessary.

Nor is there any evidence in the record or otherwise that ERCOT stands by its previous

recommendation.

        The fact that subsequent planning models assumed the 765-kV projects as part of the based

system does not establish what those models would have shown had Import Path 2 instead been

treated as the question to be tested. Neither the machinations of Applicants nor Staff can transform

an assumption embedded in a planning model into proof of the very proposition at issue in this

proceeding.

           III.     REPLY TO APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTIONS REGARDING NEED

A.      Applicants still have not established the independent necessity of Import Path 2.

        Applicants’ Exceptions repeatedly emphasize that ERCOT studied and recommended the

three import paths as an integrated transmission solution. That argument reinforces rather than

cures the PFD’s concern.

        Although the Commission must determine whether the facilities presented in this CCN

proceeding satisfy PURA § 37.056, Applicants have not attempted to establish their need in

isolation. Their own theory is that Import Path 2 is one component of an integrated, three-path

solution developed through the PBRP. If that is the basis on which Applicants ask the Commission

to find Import Path 2 necessary, then the relevant inquiry cannot stop with the fact that ERCOT

selected Import Path 2 as one piece of that larger plan. Applicants must demonstrate that the

integrated solution on which Import Path 2’s asserted need depends is itself necessary and that

Import Path 2 is a necessary component of that solution.




ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                     Page 7
            That is precisely where the distinction between the PBRP and CREZ matters. In CREZ,

the Legislature supplied the comprehensive determination that the broader transmission buildout

was necessary.         HB 5066 supplied no comparable determination for the PBRP. ERCOT’s

recommendation of an integrated transmission plan therefore cannot substitute for the statutory

showing of need required by PURA § 37.056.

           Applicants’ integration argument thus presents a problem of their own making. If the three

import paths are sufficiently interconnected that the need for Import Path 2 depends upon

construction of the broader PBRP solution, Applicants cannot establish Import Path 2’s need

without establishing the necessity of that broader solution. Conversely, if Import Path 2 can be

justified independently of the other import paths, Applicants were required to make that showing.

The PFD correctly concludes that they did not.

B.         The PFD did not improperly “retroactively apply” ERCOT’s revised load
           methodology.

           Applicants characterize the PFD as having improperly applied ERCOT’s 2025 RTP

methodology “retroactively” to the PBRP.7 That mischaracterizes the PFD. The SOAH ALJs did

not purport to amend the PBRP retroactively. They considered ERCOT’s subsequent experience

with large-load forecasting as evidence bearing on the reliability of the assumptions Applicants

now attempt to rely upon to satisfy their statutory burden under § 37.056. That is exactly what an

evidentiary hearing is supposed to do.

           ERCOT subsequently determined that officer-letter and data-center loads should be

discounted because those projected loads do not materialize at the rates previously assumed. The

relevance of that evidence does not depend upon whether ERCOT formally reopened the PBRP.



7
    Applicants’ Exceptions at 13-15.



ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                      Page 8
 It matters because Applicants ask the Commission today to commit billions of dollars of ratepayer-

funded infrastructure based substantially upon forecasts developed before those shortcomings

were recognized.

           Applicants’ argument would effectively freeze the PBRP’s factual assumptions in 2024 and

prevent the Commission from considering better evidence available at the time it actually decides

the CCN. Nothing in HB 5066 or PURA § 37.056 requires or even encourages that result.

C.         Subsequent planning documents do not prove that ERCOT reevaluated Import Path
           2 under the changed assumptions.

           Applicants repeatedly emphasize that ERCOT retained all three import paths in the

2024 RTP, 2025 RTP, and April 2026 Far West GTC exit strategy. They argue that because the

2025 RTP employed the revised forecasting methodology while continuing to include the paths,

the PFD’s changed-circumstances analysis necessarily fails. 8

           But again this confuses including an already-approved planning assumption with

independently reassessing whether that assumption remains necessary. The critical question is

whether ERCOT reran the analysis that produced the PBRP recommendation to determine whether

Import Path 2 remained necessary after applying the revised load-realization methodology to the

loads underlying the PBRP. The PFD found that no such analysis was presented.

           At its essence, Applicants are attempting to establish project-specific need by pointing to

later studies that assume the project exists. That approach defies logic and was correctly rejected

by the PFD.




8
    Applicants’ Exceptions at 15.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                       Page 9
 D.      Historical load growth does not validate the particular PBRP forecast or establish the
        need for Import Path 2.

        Applicants emphasize actual Far West load growth and argue that historical growth

independently confirms the need for additional transmission. ASL does not dispute that the

Permian Basin has experienced substantial growth or that transmission infrastructure is important

to maintaining reliability. But that is not the statutory question. The question is whether Import

Path 2 is necessary at the scale and timing proposed.

        Historical growth does not validate the specific future loads used to justify the PBRP,

particularly when those forecasts included large amounts of officer-letter, data-center,

cryptocurrency, and other loads whose realization is now subject to materially different

assumptions.

        A showing that demand has grown is not equivalent to a showing that this particular 765-

kV import path is necessary, and the ALJs correctly gave little weight to Applicants’ argument.

E.      HB 5066 required planning, it did not predetermine the solution.

        Applicants’ interpretation of HB 5066 is inconsistent with the statutory discretion correctly

recognized by the PFD. HB 5066 directed ERCOT to develop a reliability plan based on specified

information, including forecasted load. It did not direct the Commission to construct every project

appearing in that plan, waive the ordinary CCN need inquiry, or declare the 765-kV import paths

necessary as a matter of law.

        The contrast to CREZ is outcome determinative. When the Legislature intended to

predetermine need for a transmission buildout, it knew how to say so. HB 5066 contains no

comparable directive.

        Applicants’ reliance on HB 5066’s requirement for expeditious implementation likewise

cannot replace the substantive prerequisite imposed by § 37.056. Expeditious review is not


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                     Page 10
 presumed approval. The Commission must still determine whether the project is necessary on the

evidentiary record before it, just as the PFD correctly made the determination that Applicants failed

to meet its statutory burden on the record before the ALJs, who appropriately gave little weight to

the process in prior proceedings that were based on a dissimilar statutory framework.

F.      The Far West GTCs do not cure the deficiencies in the load forecast.

        Applicants characterize the Far West GTCs as an independent reliability justification for

Import Path 2, arguing that the constraints exist today regardless of future load growth. But the

PFD correctly recognized the limitation of that evidence.

        A GTC identifies a transmission-system constraint. It does not establish that the demand

driving the constraint is sufficiently durable to justify a permanent multibillion-dollar

infrastructure response.

        As the PFD explains, Applicants did not disaggregate the load driving the GTCs to address

whether it consists materially of speculative or highly price-responsive cryptocurrency load. Thus,

the GTC evidence does not validate the PBRP’s original forecast or independently demonstrate

that Import Path 2 is the necessary response to the constraint. 9

G.      Applicants’ Bell County East argument answers a different question than the PFD
        asked. 10

        Applicants improperly characterize the PFD as having incorrectly treated transmission like

a point-to-point pipeline and having improperly required Applicants to identify a particular

generator at Bell County East. That is not the PFD’s holding.




9
 PFD at 82-84.
10
  Staff raises substantially the same exception, contending that ERCOT’s statewide planning models demonstrate that
sufficient power will be available through the interconnected system to flow through Bell County East and into the
Permian Basin. ASL disagrees for the same reasons discussed herein and addresses the issue only once to avoid
unnecessary duplication. See Staff Exceptions at 12-13.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                                  Page 11
            The PFD recognized that Import Path 2 was justified as a means of importing significant

amounts of power west into the Permian Basin because the PBRP assumed insufficient local

conventional generation. The issue is not whether electricity must originate from a dedicated

generator connected to Bell County East. Rather, given the asserted purpose of Import Path 2, the

question is whether the record demonstrates that sufficient power will actually be available on the

eastern side of the path, together with sufficient transfer capability, to accomplish the function for

which the project is claimed to be necessary.

           Applicants’ generalized reliance on ERCOT’s interconnected grid does not establish that

proposition. 11 The existence of a statewide interconnected system does not, standing alone,

demonstrate that sufficient generation and transfer capability will be available to support the

westward transfers upon which the asserted need for Import Path 2 depends.

           The PFD therefore did not impose an artificial point-to-point requirement on the ERCOT

grid. It appropriately examined whether Applicants proved the factual premise underlying Import

Path 2’s asserted need: that the path will have sufficient power available to perform the function

for which Applicants contend billions of dollars in new infrastructure is necessary. Before

requiring customers and landowners to bear the cost and impacts of a multibillion-dollar import

path, Applicants should be required to establish that the path can perform the function asserted as

the basis for its necessity.




11
     See PFD at 85-87.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                      Page 12
 H.         New Permian generation is directly relevant to whether Import Path 2 remains
           necessary.

           Applicants argue that generation cannot substitute for transmission because Texas has a

competitive generation market, the Commission cannot order generators to build, and announced

projects may never materialize. 12

           But the PFD does not require the Commission to order generation development or assume

that every announced megawatt will be constructed. The point is much narrower: the record

contains credible evidence that the factual premise underlying the PBRP—that the Permian must

rely heavily on long-distance imports because it lacks sufficient local conventional generation—is

changing materially.

           The evidence is substantial. The PFD identified 25 natural-gas generation projects in the

Permian Basin and specifically noted 2,210 MW of Texas Energy Fund projects, at least 456 MW

of additional projects in the ERCOT interconnection queue, and two enormous, proposed data-

center developments totaling approximately 10,000 MW that intend to self-provide generation

rather than rely on the grid. 13

           Applicants respond that not every announced project will materialize. That may be true.

But the same uncertainty is precisely what Applicants ask the Commission to disregard when it

comes to projected load. Applicants cannot reasonably demand that speculative future load be

credited at face value while future generation capable of serving that load is dismissed because it

has not yet been constructed.

           At minimum, the evidence demonstrates that local generation is a credible alternative

warranting analysis before the Commission commits billions of dollars to a transmission solution



12
     Applicants’ Exceptions at 35-38.
13
     PFD at 94-98.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                    Page 13
 premised on importing electricity hundreds of miles into the most energy dense region in the

United States.

I.         Generation and transmission need not be mutually exclusive for generation to
           undermine Applicants’ showing of need.

           Applicants repeatedly argue that generation and transmission serve different purposes and

that local generation cannot provide the “import capability” supplied by Import Path 2. That

reasoning assumes the conclusion.

           The relevant question under § 37.056 is not whether local generation can function as a 765-

kV transmission line. Obviously it cannot. The questions is whether additional local generation

can reduce the demand for imported electricity sufficiently to reduce or eliminate the need for

Import Path 2. The PFD correctly found that intervenors presented credible evidence requiring

consideration of precisely that question. 14

           If new Permian generation serves Permian load locally, less power must be imported from

hundreds of miles away. Applicants cannot establish the necessity of an import path merely by

defining the problem as a need for “import capability” and then observing that generation does not

itself create an import path. The antecedent question is how much import capability is actually

necessary after reasonably foreseeable local generation is considered.

J.         The Commission should reject Applicants’ proposed replacement findings and
           conclusions.

           Applicants’ proposed replacement findings largely ask the Commission to convert

ERCOT’s continuing inclusion of the 765-kV paths in its planning documents into a dispositive

finding of need. The Commission should decline to do so.




14
     Id.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                      Page 14
            Those proposed findings do not cure the deficiencies identified by the PFD. They do not

establish an independent need for Import Path 2; they do not demonstrate that the PBRP load

assumptions remain reliable under after ERCOT’s revised forecasting methodology; they do not

establish that the Far West GTCs are driven by sufficiently durable load to require Import Path 2;

they do not establish adequate power available to flow west from Bell County East; and they do

not meaningfully account for the substantial conventional generation now being developed within

the Permian Basin.

             IV.     REPLY TO APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTIONS REGARDING NOTICE

           Applicants contend that the PFD’s notice analysis is inconsistent with Commission

practice, citing Docket Nos. 11014, 38597, 45624, 48358, 49523, 51023, and 59315. 15 But that

comparison ignores the defining feature of this proceeding: its unprecedented scale. The cited

proceedings involved projects spanning, respectively, one, four, two, one, three, one, and

twenty-two counties. With the exception of Docket No. 59315, none is remotely comparable to

this proceeding. Applicants cannot transform a handful of materially smaller CCN proceedings

into a settled Commission practice governing a project of this magnitude. Indeed, the PFD

appropriately recognized that the “scale and complexity” of this proceeding matter when

approximately 400 miles of new route links and 1,400 newly affected landowners were added after

the public meetings had already occurred. 16 The rule’s public-participation requirement should

not be interpreted as though adding 1,400 affected landowners is indistinguishable from an

ordinary post-meeting route adjustment.

           Docket No. 59315 does not save Applicants’ argument. ASL respectfully disagrees with

the Commission’s notice analysis in that proceeding and maintains that it should not be extended


15
     Applicants’ Exceptions at 52-53.
16
     PFD at 45.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                  Page 15
 here. Docket No. 59475 presents the issue in its starkest form: this proceeding involved an

extraordinary number of affected landowners and more than 800 intervenors. As the PFD correctly

recognized, the relevant question is not simply whether Applicants checked the minimum

procedural box of holding “at least one” meeting, but whether the approximately 1,400 landowners

brought into the project afterward received the pre-filing opportunity for community input

contemplated by Rule 22.52(a)(4). 17

           Applicants’ proposed solution—if it can meaningfully be called one—only underscores

why the notice deficiency cannot be cured at this stage of the proceeding. Applicants assert that if

additional process is warranted, “the answer is to provide additional process.” 18 But Applicants

never explain what meaningful “additional process” could now restore. The public meetings were

intended to occur before filing, while community input could still inform route development. The

application has since been filed, parties intervened, discovery occurred, testimony was filed, and

the merits hearing concluded. Providing “additional process” now cannot recreate the opportunity

to participate before Applicants selected the routes presented to the Commission. Applicants’

suggestion therefore proves the PFD’s point: the prejudice cannot be cured merely by adding more

procedure to an already completed record.

           And if Applicants truly believe that additional process is necessary to cure the deficiencies

in this unprecedented proceeding, that position reinforces ASL’s Motion to Abate, which the

Commission has yet to directly address, and on which Staff has remained conspicuously silent.

The appropriate response to procedural inadequacy on this scale is not to approve the project first

and attempt to manufacture additional process after the fact. At minimum, it demonstrates why

these unprecedented 765-kV proceedings should be abated or denied so that a process capable of


17
     Id. at 44.
18
     Applicants’ Exceptions at 75.


ASL’s Reply to Exceptions                                                                        Page 16
 providing meaningful participation can be established before the Commission authorizes

infrastructure affecting thousands of Texas landowners.

                                      V.    CONCLUSION

        For these reasons, ASL respectfully requests that the SOAH ALJs deny Staff’s and

Applicants’ Exceptions regarding need and notice, adhere to the PFD’s recommended findings and

conclusions on need and notice, and continue to recommend denial of the applications filed in

Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475.

                                             Respectfully submitted,
